clue.text: Name muscle-bound actor as Fairy Godmother

indicators.note: Bound means tied up and held fast, so the letter beside it cannot sit alongside the word for muscle — it is tied up inside it.

parts.note: beef is muscle, both the meat and the bulk a weightlifter puts on
N is the standard abbreviation for name, the one printed on a form
a female actor is an actress, which is how the setter gets the feminine ending

explanation.walkthrough: 'Muscle-bound' looks like one word describing the performer. It is really two jobs at once: a word meaning muscle, and an order to tie something up inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fairy Godmother -> BENEFACTRESS: the storybook example of a woman who showers money and favours on someone, which is what the word names.

clue.text: Peel tuber for cooking programme

indicators.note: cooking means preparing and mixing up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A kitchen instruction to skin a potato ready for cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooking programme' reads as a TV food show, but 'cooking' rearranges the letters and 'programme' alone is the definition. Blue Peter is a long-running BBC children's television show.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue Peter is a British children's TV show on the BBC since 1958, so it is a programme.

clue.text: Official witness to any Republican dodges

indicators.note: To dodge is to duck and weave and never stay put, so the letters in front will not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: five of the six letters come straight off the page, waiting to be reordered
R is the standard abbreviation for a US Republican

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a politician evading awkward questions. 'Official witness to any Republican' reads as one long job description, which is where the definition looks longer than it is — it stops after two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Official witness -> NOTARY: a notary public is the officer licensed to witness signatures and certify documents, so the phrase names the job.

clue.text: Cross journalist covering conflict sent on to another

indicators.note: To cover something is to lie over it and hide it from view, so the word for conflict vanishes inside the letters either side of it.

parts.note: to cross a stream on foot is to ford it
ED is the crossword's standing journalist, short for editor
a war is an armed conflict

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' wants to be the adjective meaning annoyed, matching the angry journalist of the surface. It is the verb, and a ford is a place where you cross.
explanation.definitionFit: sent on to another -> FORWARDED: a letter or an email passed along to a new recipient has been forwarded, the verb for relaying something you were sent.

clue.text: Long line of cars?

parts.note: the reading the surface offers is traffic: a tailback of vehicles stretching away up the road; the setter's cars are the ones that hang from a moving steel rope up a mountainside or a San Francisco hill, and it is the rope being described

explanation.walkthrough: No wordplay to separate out here — the whole clue is one description, and the joke is that a line of cars can mean a mountain lift rather than a traffic jam.
explanation.definitionFit: Long line of cars? -> CABLE: the continuous rope hauling a cable car is a very long line, and the cars are named after it.

clue.text: Dark hens fancy one with colourful legs

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are arranged in a new way

explanation.surface: A poultry keeper's fancy for a dark-feathered breed with bright legs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' reads as a verb of liking, but it rearranges the letters of DARK HENS.
explanation.definitionFit: The redshank is a wading bird named for its bright orange-red legs.

clue.text: Fleece as thin as tights, you'd say

indicators.note: The phrase hands the clue to the ear: what matters is the noise you would make out loud, not the spelling you would write down.

parts.note: tights thin enough to see through are sheer, and that word said aloud is written a second way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleece' looks like the noun, a woolly thing being compared with tights. It is the verb, and the joke is that a fleece is exactly what comes off under the clippers.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleece -> SHEAR: to fleece a sheep is to clip the wool off it, the plain farming sense of the verb rather than the swindling one the surface suggests.

clue.text: Charming party held by great guy you hardly know

indicators.note: Whatever is held by something ends up inside it, so the two pieces named first are set within the piece named after these words.

parts.note: ace is slang for great or first-rate, and it splits to take the others in
quaint is charming in an old-fashioned, slightly odd way
the ANC is South Africa's governing political party, the African National Congress

explanation.walkthrough: 'Held by great guy' reads as a single phrase about one generous host, which is the trap: 'great' is doing its own separate job and the definition is only the last four words.
explanation.definitionFit: guy you hardly know -> ACQUAINTANCE: someone you know slightly and no better, the word English keeps for exactly that distance short of friendship.

clue.text: Collect Charlie Sheen on Wall Street?

indicators.note: Wall Street is in New York, so the word in front of it is to be spelled the American way rather than the British one.

parts.note: C is Charlie in the NATO alphabet used by pilots and radio operators
a sheen is a soft gloss — lustre in Britain, luster in America

explanation.walkthrough: Charlie Sheen is an actor and Wall Street is one of his films, so the surface reads as a name and a title. The clue wants the two words separated and the spelling changed.
explanation.definitionFit: Collect -> CLUSTER: things that collect around a point form a cluster, the verb sense of gathering into one tight group.

clue.text: University replacing last of cheap parking to make room

indicators.note: replacing says the university letter takes the place of another
last of points to the final letter of the cheap word

parts.note: budget means cheap, as in a budget airline
the final letter that is swapped out
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A university swaps out its cheap car park to free up space.
explanation.walkthrough: U replaces the T at the end of BUDGET, and P follows. Budge up is British for shuffle along to let someone sit.
explanation.definitionFit: To budge up is to move along a bench or seat to make space for another person.

clue.text: Gift wrapping season, November's advance warning

indicators.note: Wrapping paper goes round the outside of what it covers, so the word for gift closes over the two pieces that follow it.

parts.note: a present is a gift, and only its final letter is left on the far side of the wrapping
a season is a particular stretch of the year, and any stretch like that is a time
N is November in the NATO alphabet; the possessive 's is only the sentence joining up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gift wrapping season' says December and 'November' says the month before it, so the whole surface is a Christmas picture. Neither month is what the wordplay wants.
explanation.definitionFit: advance warning -> PRESENTIMENT: a presentiment is a feeling that something is about to happen, so it warns you before there is anything to see.

clue.text: Capital, winning an event

parts.note: a side that is winning is up, as in two goals up
per stands in for 'a' or 'an' in phrases like five pounds a head
a case is an instance or occurrence — in any event, in any case

explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' is the trap: with 'winning an event' beside it, it wants to be a city or a fortune. Here it is the printer's sense, a capital letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital -> UPPER CASE: a capital letter came from the upper of the two trays of type a compositor kept, the small letters living in the lower one.

clue.text: Migrants coming through Sandwich or Deal

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular: the word names one crowd made up of many people, so the setter is defining the mass by its members.

indicators.note: People coming through a town pass right across it without stopping, and the letters wanted do the same — they run unbroken across the words.

parts.note: Sandwich and Deal are neighbouring towns on the Kent coast, and five letters in a row inside these three words are what is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Sandwich and Deal look like lunch and a bargain, which is the joke. Both are real Kent towns a few miles from the Channel, so the surface reads as a news bulletin.
explanation.definitionFit: Migrants -> HORDE: a horde is a large body of people on the move, originally a wandering tribe, so it names migrants taken together as one mass.

clue.text: Hot on piebald horse, wiping head

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter at the front of it, and wiping that off leaves the rest of the word standing.

parts.note: a pinto is the American horse with irregular white patches — piebald, in other words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot on' is the definition and looks like more of the riding picture, an eager rider on a spotted pony. Both halves pull the same way, which is what makes the join hard to find.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot on -> INTO: to be into something is to be keen on it, and 'hot on' is the same slangy way of saying you are enthusiastic about a subject.

clue.text: Very tough mother opposed to ibuprofen finally admitted to A&E

indicators.note: admitted to, like a patient, places the other pieces inside

parts.note: the letters A and E, as in the hospital department
a dam is an animal's mother
anti means opposed to

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of ibuprofen

parts.note: the word whose last letter N is taken

explanation.surface: A tough mother, against painkillers, is taken into hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E, Accident and Emergency, is the British hospital casualty department; 'admitted to' puts the other pieces between its two letters, and 'finally' gives the last letter of ibuprofen.
explanation.definitionFit: Adamantine means as hard as adamant, an unbreakable legendary stone, so unyielding and very tough.

clue.text: Pieces' pieces?

definitions.meaning: the first word means whole works — a symphony, a sonata, a quartet — each written and performed as one piece of music
the second means the self-contained sections such a work divides into, the numbered parts a concert programme lists with their tempo markings

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart: the clue is one idea said twice, using the same word in two musical senses and letting the apostrophe do the joining.
explanation.definitionFit: Pieces' pieces? -> MOVEMENTS: a symphony is built out of self-contained sections, so the parts of a musical work are themselves pieces of music.

clue.text: Start filling Aussie's truck, carrying melons to the north

indicators.note: carrying means holding within, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: to be filling a truck is to be in it
a ute is an Australian pickup truck, short for utility vehicle

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north reads the word upwards, i.e. backwards

parts.note: melons and tits are both slang for breasts

explanation.surface: Someone begins loading an Australian pickup with melons heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start filling' looks like the instruction, but 'Start' is the definition, a verb. 'filling Aussie's truck' gives IN UTE, which carries STIT, TITS read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: To institute something is to set it up or begin it, so to start it.

clue.text: Thump insensitive bigmouth

parts.note: a thump is a blow, the kind struck with a fist
a hard man is insensitive, unmoved by anything around him

explanation.walkthrough: Two plain synonyms laid end to end with nothing to mark the join, and a surface that reads as one continuous description of an unpleasant person.
explanation.definitionFit: bigmouth -> BLOWHARD: a blowhard boasts loudly and endlessly, which is exactly the charge in calling someone a bigmouth.

clue.text: True love juggling with two donations — just the first of those?

definitions.text: True love juggling with two donations — just the first of those?

indicators.note: A juggler keeps everything moving and nothing where it started, so the letters handed over land in a different arrangement.
'Those' points back at the two words already named, and only the letter each one begins with is taken from them.

parts.note: eight of the ten letters come from these two words
the opening letter of each of these two words makes up the shortfall

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: every word is wordplay, and the same words read straight are the definition. The dash is the hinge, and 'those' looks back rather than forward.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines: in the Twelve Days of Christmas the true love's second gift is two of these birds, and the clue asks for just one of them.

clue.text: Secret alert, with ship in port unloading gold

indicators.note: in places the ship letters inside what is left
unloading means taking cargo off, so the gold letters are removed

parts.note: taken as a word for a harbour town
or is gold in heraldry
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A quiet warning that a ship in harbour is offloading gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unloading' takes OR out of PORT, leaving PT, and the ship SS goes 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Psst is the hushed sound used to catch someone's attention secretly.

clue.text: Break — nearly all want one in Rome

indicators.note: nearly all keeps the word for want but its final letter

parts.note: want means lack
the final letter dropped
una is Italian for one, in the feminine

explanation.surface: Taking a break in Rome, nearly everyone wants one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly all' trims LACK to LAC. Una is the Italian for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A lacuna is a gap or missing section, a break in a text or sequence.

clue.text: Recognise Thatcherite Chancellor on the radio? Not at all

indicators.note: Radio reaches you as sound and nothing else, so both names are to be heard rather than read off the page.

parts.note: to recognise something is to know it, and said aloud that word loses its silent K
Geoffrey Howe was Margaret Thatcher's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Britain's finance minister, and his name is said exactly like the question word

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are heard rather than spelled, and neither is written the way it sounds. The surface asks whether you would place the man's voice on air.
explanation.definitionFit: Not at all -> NOHOW: nohow is the dialect emphatic for in no way whatever, as in 'that won't work nohow'.

clue.text: Where shoes may have to be removed, socks protecting you?

definitions.text: Where shoes may have to be removed

indicators.note: Something protecting you is wrapped right round you, so the single letter standing for the person goes inside the other word.

parts.note: hose is the old collective word for socks and stockings, still alive in hosiery
U is the textspeak short form of you, and crosswords use it freely

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is one tidy hallway scene. The question mark is the warning: 'socks protecting you' has stopped describing and started instructing.
explanation.definitionFit: Where shoes may have to be removed -> HOUSE: in many countries, and in plenty of homes anywhere, shoes come off at the front door.

clue.text: Space to work out my amusing anagrams

indicators.note: anagrams is used as a verb: the phrase that follows is turned into a rearrangement of itself

explanation.surface: A boast that one's clever word games give the brain a workout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anagrams' is a verb here: MY AMUSING rearranges into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnasium is a hall equipped for physical exercise, a place where people go to train.

clue.text: Pick up good tip

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good, as on a school report
to tip is to lean, the way a ladder tips against a wall

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pick up' looks like part of the same instruction as 'tip', as though something were being lifted and tilted. It is the definition, standing on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Pick up -> GLEAN: to glean is to gather the stray grain left after harvest, and by extension to pick up scraps of information here and there.

clue.text: Fast runner passed rival

parts.note: the Australian bird cannot fly but sprints at close to 50km/h
the late Mr So-and-so is the one who has passed away

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast runner passed' reads as one athlete overtaking another, which is the whole misdirection: 'passed' is the euphemism for died, not the move on the track.
explanation.definitionFit: rival -> EMULATE: both verbs mean to match someone by measuring yourself against them, the answer adding the sense of copying in order to do it.

clue.text: Pacific Islander going east or west?

definitions.text: Pacific Islander going east or west?

parts.words: Pacific Islander going east or west?
parts.note: an islander whose name reads the same whichever way, east or west, an across entry is read

explanation.surface: A puzzle about which way a Pacific traveller is heading.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the trick: the islander's name is a palindrome, the same whether read eastward (left to right) or westward.
explanation.definitionFit: Nauru is a tiny island nation in the Pacific, and its people are Nauruans.

clue.text: Charge fellow spreading faeces for pig

parts.note: a fee is a charge
a don is a fellow of a university college

indicators.note: spreading means smearing about, so the letters of faeces are rearranged

explanation.surface: A farmer bills a man for muck-spreading in the pigsty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pig' is a verb here, not the farmyard animal: to eat greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: To feed one's face is to eat greedily, which is what pigging out means.
